chapter.name: The Story of Indian Farming
chapter.blurb: India's agricultural landscape, early farming, climate and monsoon, kharif-rabi-zaid, soils, soil and water care, seeds and farming methods, government support and challenges.

concepts.name: India's agricultural landscape
concepts.description: The meaning of agriculture and allied activities, its share in the economy and employment, and the role of women farmers.
concepts.idea: Agriculture includes farming, livestock, forestry and horticulture and supports nearly half of India's workers.
concepts.rule: Agriculture is one of the oldest occupations and includes preparing soil, growing plants, rearing livestock and growing trees; some farmers also rear fish or silk cocoons. Broadly it covers farming, animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture. The word comes from Latin: agri means field and culture means to cultivate. The government classifies it as agriculture and allied activities, including livestock, beekeeping, fisheries, silkworm rearing and fibre production. In 2022-23 a little over 18 per cent of India's GDP came from agriculture and allied activities, and about 46 per cent of the working population depends on them. In rural India more than 75 per cent of those working in agriculture are women.
concepts.example: Wheat fields in Punjab, saffron in Kashmir and tea in the Nilgiris show India's varied farming.

concepts.name: Echoes from the past: early crops and farming texts
concepts.description: Prehistoric farming, early crops, intercropping at Kalibangan, domestication and ancient texts on agriculture.
concepts.idea: Indian farming is prehistoric, and ancient texts record advanced knowledge of seeds, soil and grafting.
concepts.rule: Rice grains in the Ganga plain date to the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, and barley and millets at Mehrgarh to the 7th millennium BCE. Farmers later grew oilseeds, legumes, fibre crops, vegetables and fruits. The Vedas mention yava (barley), godhuma (wheat) and vrihi (rice). Intercropping at Kalibangan around 2800 BCE is seen from perpendicular furrows. Animals were domesticated from about 3500 BCE. Texts such as Kautilya's Arthashastra, Sangam literature, Krishiparashara, Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita and Surapala's Vrikshayurveda give agricultural knowledge; the Brihatsamhita describes a grafting method still used.
concepts.example: Surapala advised watering newly planted trees in arid land morning and evening for fifteen days.

concepts.name: Climate, agroclimatic zones and the monsoon in agriculture
concepts.description: How climate shapes crops, the 15 agroclimatic zones and the role of the southwest and northeast monsoons.
concepts.idea: India's varied climate and monsoons decide what can be grown where and when.
concepts.rule: Xuanzang noted that produce differs with climate and soil. India has seven climate types: alpine, temperate, subtropical, arid, tropical wet, semi-arid and tropical. India is divided into 15 agroclimatic zones, made by combining climate, soil, terrain and vegetation, which helps plan what, when and how to grow crops. The southwest monsoon brings rain from June to September, crucial for kharif crops in the north and centre. The northeast monsoon from October to December brings rain to the east and south. Malabar and Coromandel coasts get both, so the south can grow crops in between. Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh grow rice all year with monsoon and irrigation.
concepts.example: In the dry season northern farmers use groundwater, rivers, canals and ponds.

concepts.name: Kharif, rabi and zaid crops
concepts.description: The three cropping seasons, their crops, timing and challenges.
concepts.idea: India has three cropping seasons: kharif in the monsoon, rabi in winter and zaid in summer.
concepts.rule: Indian agriculture is mainly divided into kharif, rabi and zaid, terms of Arabic origin used since Mughal times. Earlier names were kedara (wet crops), haimana (winter crops) and graishmika (summer crops). Kharif crops, sown with the monsoon, include rice, maize, jowar, bajra, sugarcane, groundnut and cotton. Rabi crops, winter crops sown in cool weather, include wheat, barley, peas, mustard and gram. Zaid crops grown in summer include watermelon, cucumber, muskmelon and pumpkin. Kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of monsoon, and excessive rainfall destroys them.
concepts.example: Mustard and wheat are rabi crops; pearl millet is a kharif crop.

concepts.name: Soil: formation and the six major soil types
concepts.description: How soil forms, humus, the six soil types of India and their crops.
concepts.idea: Soil forms over centuries from rocks and organic matter, and India has six main types.
concepts.rule: Soil is the thin upper layer of Earth's crust that supports plants, formed over millions of years by breakdown of rocks and decay of organic matter. Humus, dark organic matter from decomposed plants and animals, is rich in nutrients and holds moisture. The Amarakosha describes twelve kinds of agricultural land. The six major soils are alluvial, black, red, laterite, desert and mountain/alpine. Alluvial soil is silt deposited by rivers and is rich in nutrients. Black or cotton soil, from weathered volcanic rocks, holds moisture and is fertile. Red soil, from lava or old rocks, is red because of iron and is not very fertile. Laterite soil, from weathering by rain, hardens in heat and is not fertile. Alpine soil is thin, rough and rocky.
concepts.example: Black soil is also called cotton soil.

concepts.name: Nurturing soil and water: conservation and irrigation
concepts.description: Soil conservation techniques, rain-fed and irrigated farming, traditional and modern irrigation.
concepts.idea: Farmers protect soil with rotation and terracing and use rain-fed and irrigated methods.
concepts.rule: Healthy soil holds bacteria, fungi, earthworms, minerals, humus, water and air. Traditional conservation includes crop rotation, multiple cropping, contour ploughing and organic fertilisers such as cow dung; panchagavya is a fermented mixture of five cow products. Modern methods include terracing, afforestation, mulching and ploughing back crop residue. Rain-fed farming relies entirely on rainfall, facing droughts and unpredictable monsoons. Irrigated farming supplies water artificially. Traditional systems include kull, kund, ahar, pokhar, khadin, arakere, eri, phad systems of Maharashtra and bamboo drip irrigation in the northeast. Kallanai was built about 1,800 years ago. Drip irrigation delivers water to roots through tubes; sprinklers spray water like rain.
concepts.example: Banana trees on paddy bunds act as windbreakers and hold soil.

concepts.name: Seeds, traditional and contemporary farming, and sustainable pathways
concepts.description: Seeds, beejamrit, the Indian seed drill, traditional systems, the Green Revolution, its limits, organic farming and Sikkim.
concepts.idea: Traditional wisdom and the Green Revolution each have strengths, and sustainable farming combines them.
concepts.rule: Seeds have been passed down and shared in families and communities. ICAR developed beejamrit, a paste of cow dung and urine, to coat seeds. The ancient Indian seed drill combined soil preparation, sowing and closing the furrow. Company seeds give higher yield but may not be suitable for replanting, creating dependence. Traditional farming treats plant and soil as one system; examples are terrace farming, kulagar (Konkan homestead farming) and gokrishi. ICAR documented almost 5,000 traditional practices and found over 85 per cent validated by modern science. The Green Revolution of the 1960s-70s brought HYV seeds, irrigation, chemicals and machinery, making India self-sufficient in food, but caused soil impoverishment, groundwater depletion and contamination. Sustainable farming includes organic farming and neem pesticides. Sikkim became the world's first 100 per cent organic state in 2014.
concepts.example: M.S. Swaminathan was the architect of the Green Revolution.

questions.q: Was the Green Revolution a success? Justify.
questions.a: It made India self-sufficient in food but caused long-term harm to soil and water, so its success is mixed.

questions.q: Design a poster promoting organic farming in your village with three messages.
questions.a: A poster with messages such as use compost, avoid chemicals and protect bees and soil.

concepts.name: The role of the government and the challenges farmers face
concepts.description: Government support for farmers, hydroponics, and challenges such as small landholdings, climate change, the Ganga basin and debt.
concepts.idea: The government supports farmers, yet small holdings, climate change and debt threaten farming.
concepts.rule: The government helps farmers with seeds, fertilisers, weather forecasts, research and training, cheaper electricity for irrigation and crop insurance such as the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana. It buys important crops at fair prices and promotes cold storage and digital markets. Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water without soil. Challenges include shrinking landholdings (average about three-fourths of a hectare), difficulty using expensive machines, low incomes, climate change with untimely rains and extreme events, and a stressed Ganga basin serving over 500 million people. Loans can create a debt trap, and as many as 2,300 farmers a day may abandon agriculture.
concepts.example: The average landholding is about the size of a football field.

questions.q: Why do many farm families have other sources of income?
questions.a: They rear cows, goats and poultry, keep bees, fish and collect forest produce, since crops alone may not give enough income; diversity builds resilience.

questions.q: Why is the Ganga under stress?
questions.a: Glaciers melt fast, water is diverted to irrigation, groundwater is pumped and hundreds of dams block flow.

questions.q: Explain why climate change is a special challenge for farmers.
questions.a: Weather becomes unpredictable with untimely rains and extreme events, so crops are more likely to be destroyed and losses are heavy.

questions.q: Compare hydroponics with traditional soil farming.
questions.a: Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient water in controlled settings without soil, while traditional farming uses soil and natural cycles.

questions.q: Explain how digital technology and cold storage help farmers.
questions.a: Cold storage keeps produce fresh, and digital technology gives access to information and markets, so farmers get better prices.

questions.q: What is the most important step to help small farmers? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned choice such as fair prices, insurance or small machines suitable for small farms.

questions.q: Write a short speech to your village on ways to strengthen farming.
questions.a: A speech urging use of insurance, water saving, diversified income and sustainable methods.
